title: Five Readings of the Strait of Hormuz on the Same 24-Hour Window: Kpler 5 / Windward 12 / CENTCOM 55 / Iran Tasnim and Fars Zero. The Mediators Who Announced 'Encouraging Progress' Cited None of Them. Iran's Own Government Told State Media Not to Portray the Closure and the Talks as Contradictory.
narrative:
On 22 June 2026 — within hours of mediators Pakistan and Qatar announcing the Bürgenstock Day-1 round produced 'encouraging progress' and a 60-day roadmap — three independent shipping-data providers, the US military, and Iran's own news agencies issued mutually exclusive statements about the Strait of Hormuz on the same 24-hour window.

The Pakistan–Qatar joint mediator statement on 22 June said the parties had established 'a communication line … to avoid incidents and miscommunication with the aim of safe passage for commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz,' citing paragraph 5 of the 14-point MoU signed 17 June by Trump and Pezeshkian.

CENTCOM on 21 June reported 55 merchant vessels carrying approximately 17M barrels transited the strait on Saturday — 'traffic up, not down.'

Iran's Tasnim News Agency on Sunday, citing maritime navigation data, reported no vessels had passed through since Iran's military declared closure on 20 June. The IRGC Navy via Fars News Agency escalated: the strait 'remains closed, and the IRGC Navy will not issue any permits for vessel passage until further notice.' Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority issued guidance: 'no vessel is permitted to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without a valid passage permit.'

Kpler on 22 June reported only 5 vessels transited Sunday, down from 26 Saturday. Windward reported 12 vessels Sunday (down from 35 Saturday), with 5 of 8 inbound vessels running dark (AIS off).

Iran's Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), per an internal directive obtained by Iran International, instructed state media on Saturday not to portray the renewed closure and simultaneous participation in talks as a 'split' between the 'field' and diplomacy.

sources: Pakistan–Qatar joint mediator statement, 22 June 2026 — 'a communication line … to avoid incidents and miscommunication with the aim of safe passage for commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz,' citing MoU paragraph 5
CENTCOM statement, 21 June 2026 — 55 merchant vessels, ~17M barrels transited Saturday, 'traffic up, not down'
Iran Tasnim News Agency, Sunday 22 June — no vessels passed through since IRGC military declared closure on 20 June
Fars News Agency, Sunday 22 June, IRGC Navy military source — 'The Strait of Hormuz remains closed, and the IRGC Navy will not issue any permits for vessel passage until further notice'
Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority guidance — 'no vessel is permitted to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without a valid passage permit'
Kpler shipping data via Reuters/Splash247/Iran International, 22 June 2026 — 5 vessels Sunday, down from 26 Saturday
Windward shipping data, X post — 12 vessels Sunday (down from 35 Saturday), with 5 of 8 inbound vessels running dark (AIS off)

Iran Supreme National Security Council internal directive obtained by Iran International, Saturday — instructed state media 'do not portray the renewed closure and Iran's simultaneous participation in talks as a split'
Vance statement to CNBC, pre-talks — 'no evidence' of strait closure
Lloyd's marine war risk consortium launch (Chubb-led), 19 June 2026, $400M cover
ADNOC and Kuwait Petroleum Corp tenders selling crude with option to load from inside OR outside the Strait
The National (UAE) — three India-flagged tankers 'seen no [indication of the strait] being closed'

analysis:
Four findings from the cross-referenced primary sources make the 22 June five-source Hormuz reading a beat-distinct piece from prior Iran-deal Hormuz coverage (20 June 'first step' closure with CENTCOM 55/17M, 21 June 'instantly reopened' vs Intertanko central-route-closed, Burgenstock Day 1 opening piece).

**Finding 1 — Five readings of the same strait in 24 hours.** CENTCOM (US): 55 ships / 17M barrels Saturday — open. Kpler (industry): 26 ships Saturday, 5 ships Sunday. Windward (industry): 35 ships Saturday, 12 Sunday, 5 of 8 inbound dark. Iran Tasnim/Fars (official): zero Saturday, zero Sunday, IRGC Navy issuing no permits. Iran SNSC directive: closure is 'support for' the negotiation, not contradiction. These five readings cannot all be true simultaneously.

**Finding 2 — The SNSC directive is the load-bearing document.** Iran's own government told its state media 'do not portray the renewed closure and Iran's simultaneous participation in talks as a split.' The directive proves the Iranian government was managing the contradiction in real time — five numerical readings from sources on the same Iranian side that the public closure and the public negotiation are part of the same strategy. Without the directive, the five readings could be dismissed as data discrepancies; with it, the Iranian government itself confirms the closure is intentional and coordinated with the talks.

**Finding 3 — MoU paragraph 5 vs the Iranian Strait Authority permit regime.** MoU paragraph 5 commits Iran to 'best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels with no charge, for 60 days only.' Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority guidance says 'no vessel is permitted to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without a valid passage permit.' These are not the same regime — Iran is operationalizing 'best efforts' as discretionary permit issuance. The MoU paragraph does not mention a permit regime; the Iranian permit regime is unilateral. The IRGC Navy 'will not issue any permits for vessel passage until further notice' is the operational consequence: paragraph 5 has no enforcement mechanism and Iran is the gatekeeper of the discretionary layer.

**Finding 4 — The producer hedge proves the operators price in the closure.** ADNOC and Kuwait Petroleum Corp issued tenders selling crude with option to load from inside OR outside the Strait. Producers — the parties whose revenue depends on shipping — pricing in the closure risk the mediator statement denies. Lloyd's launched a new marine war risk consortium (Chubb-led) on 19 June with $400M cover — the insurance industry's verdict is that the strait remains a war-risk zone 30+ days after the MoU. Kpler's 5 Sunday transits were 19% of the post-MoU Thursday peak (25) and 4% of pre-war baseline (130–160 vessels/day).

**Vance's 'no evidence' vs the IRGC Navy's 'no permits' — both literally true.** From Washington, no visible closure infrastructure. From Bandar Abbas, no permit issuance. The two statements measure different things: physical closure vs administrative authorization. The mediator statement cites neither measurement and the SNSC directive confirms the contradiction was visible from within Iran.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: On 21–22 June 2026, five independent sources — Kpler, Windward, CENTCOM, Iran Tasnim/Fars, and the Iran SNSC directive via Iran International — gave five different operational pictures of the Strait of Hormuz on the same 24-hour window. Kpler's 5 Sunday is the load-bearing figure: 19% of the post-MoU Thursday peak (25) and 4% of pre-war baseline (130–160 vessels/day). The SNSC directive is the load-bearing document — Iran's own government told its media to lie about the closure being contradictory to the talks because the contradiction was visible. MoU paragraph 5's 'best efforts' is operationalized as discretionary permit issuance by the IRGC Navy; the Strait Authority guidance makes the permit regime unilateral and unaccountable to the paragraph. Vance's 'no evidence' and the IRGC Navy's 'no permits' are both literally true from different vantage points: from Washington, no visible closure infrastructure; from Bandar Abbas, no permit issuance. The mediator statement was honest about the negotiation; it was not honest about the strait. The 22 June five-source constellation is the first Day-1-of-talks evidence that the mediators' 'encouraging progress' framing and the strait's operational reality cannot be reconciled on the same day.
